Logistic regression trees with glmtree

Adrien Ehrhardt

2026-10-11

Source: vignettes/glmtree.Rmd
glmtree.Rmd

A logistic regression tree is a decision tree whose leaves hold logistic regressions: the tree cuts the population into segments, and each segment gets its own scoring function. glmtree searches such a tree with a stochastic EM algorithm where the segment of each observation is a latent variable (see the manuscript linked in the README). This vignette shows the interface on the two simulated settings of generateData(), and compares with a single logistic regression and with the model-based recursive partitioning of partykit::glmtree().

library(glmtree)

When there is a tree: three segments, three regressions

In the "tree" scenario the sign of the effect of x2 and x3 depends on a categorical feature x1 (its six levels come in three pairs), so a single logistic regression is misspecified.

data <- generateData(n = 2000, scenario = "tree")
train <- sample(nrow(data), 1400)
features <- c("x1", "x2", "x3")
fit <- glmtree(
  x = data[train, features], y = data$y[train],
  K = 5, iterations = 100,
  ctree_controls = partykit::ctree_control(alpha = 0.1, minbucket = 80, maxdepth = 4)
)
fit
#> Logistic regression tree fitted by SEM
#>   segments: 3 | best iteration: 35 of 100 
#>   bic of the best tree: -1463 (training set)
#> 
#> Model formula:
#> .segment ~ x1 + x2 + x3
#> 
#> Fitted party:
#> [1] root
#> |   [2] x1 in 1, 2, 3, 4
#> |   |   [3] x3 <= 0.49388: 3 (n = 583, err = 47.7%)
#> |   |   [4] x3 > 0.49388: 4 (n = 359, err = 62.1%)
#> |   [5] x1 in 5, 6
#> |   |   [6] x1 in 5
#> |   |   |   [7] x2 <= 0.55806: 5 (n = 151, err = 1.3%)
#> |   |   |   [8] x2 > 0.55806: 5 (n = 85, err = 56.5%)
#> |   |   [9] x1 in 6
#> |   |   |   [10] x2 <= -0.33494: 5 (n = 96, err = 47.9%)
#> |   |   |   [11] x2 > -0.33494: 5 (n = 126, err = 29.4%)
#> 
#> Number of inner nodes:    5
#> Number of terminal nodes: 6

predict() gives the probability of the positive class (or, with type = "segment", the segment) of new observations; the fitted tree is fit@best.tree$tree (a partykit object that can be plotted) and the logistic regression of each segment is in fit@best.tree$glms.

table(true_cluster = data$c[-train], segment = predict(fit, data[-train, features], type = "segment"))
#>             segment
#> true_cluster   3   4   5
#>            1 127  68   0
#>            2 130  65   0
#>            3   0   0 210
plot(fit@best.tree$tree)

The evolution of the criterion along the chain (here the BIC, computed on the training set, higher is better) shows when the chain settles; only iterations after the burn-in can be selected.

plot(unlist(fit@performance$criterionEvolution), type = "l", xlab = "Iteration", ylab = "-BIC")
abline(v = fit@performance$best_iteration, lty = 2)

We compare the test-set Gini index (2 AUC - 1) with a single logistic regression and with partykit::glmtree() (model-based recursive partitioning, MOB), which looks for splits by a parameter instability test instead of a likelihood-based latent variable.

logit <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = data[train, ], family = binomial)
mob <- partykit::glmtree(y ~ x2 + x3 | x1 + x2 + x3, data = data[train, ], family = binomial)
c(
  logit = normalizedGini(data$y[-train], predict(logit, data[-train, ], type = "response")),
  mob = normalizedGini(data$y[-train], predict(mob, data[-train, ], type = "response")),
  glmtree = normalizedGini(data$y[-train], predict(fit, data[-train, features]))
)
#>     logit       mob   glmtree 
#> 0.1917357 0.6472518 0.6169301

When there is no tree: apparent clusters but a single regression

In the "no tree" scenario the features form three clusters, but y depends on them through one logistic regression. There is nothing to gain from segmenting, and a good method should not lose much by trying.

data <- generateData(n = 2000, scenario = "no tree")
train <- sample(nrow(data), 1400)
fit <- glmtree(
  x = data[train, c("x1", "x2")], y = data$y[train], K = 5, iterations = 100,
  ctree_controls = partykit::ctree_control(alpha = 0.1, minbucket = 80, maxdepth = 4)
)
logit <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = data[train, ], family = binomial)
c(
  logit = normalizedGini(data$y[-train], predict(logit, data[-train, ], type = "response")),
  glmtree = normalizedGini(data$y[-train], predict(fit, data[-train, c("x1", "x2")]))
)
#>     logit   glmtree 
#> 0.6652462 0.6634425

Choosing the best tree

The chain draws many trees. Which one is returned depends on criterion ("bic", "aic" or "gini") and on where it is computed:

  • by default (validation = FALSE) the AIC or BIC of the training data is used (each segment pays for its parameters, the BIC of a segment uses the logarithm of its size);
  • with validation = TRUE a fraction proportions of the data is held out and the log-likelihood (no penalty is needed) or the Gini index is computed there at each iteration;
  • with test = TRUE another fraction is held out, never used for selection, on which the criterion of the best tree is reported in fit@performance$performance; proportions = c(test, validation) when both are used.

burn_in is the number of first iterations that cannot be selected, and patience stops the chain when the criterion has not improved for that many iterations.

fit <- glmtree(
  x = data[, features], y = data$y, test = TRUE, validation = TRUE,
  proportions = c(0.2, 0.2), criterion = "gini", patience = 50
)

Comparison with a clustering of the features

A popular alternative is to cluster the observations on their features (for instance on the first principal components) and fit one regression per cluster. This only helps when the clusters of the features are related to the heterogeneity of the response, which is not the case in the "tree" scenario: the response depends on the segment through x1, which a PCA of the features does not isolate.

data <- generateData(n = 2000, scenario = "tree")
train <- sample(nrow(data), 1400)
mixed <- FactoMineR::FAMD(data[train, features], graph = FALSE)
cluster <- function(newdata) stats::predict(mixed, newdata)$coord[, "Dim 1"] < 0
segment <- cluster(data[, features])
pred <- numeric(nrow(data))
for (j in c(TRUE, FALSE)) {
  model <- glm(y ~ x1 + x2 + x3, data = data[train, ][segment[train] == j, ], family = binomial)
  pred[segment == j] <- predict(model, data[segment == j, ], type = "response")
}
normalizedGini(data$y[-train], pred[-train])
#> [1] 0.4744621
